prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: The round-1 exchange has not weakened my view that B006 is the strongest case on the shortlist, and all six of us now agree on that. The chain from proglucagon processing, to the insulinotropic truncated peptide, to human incretin physiology and receptor biology, to durable agonists with benefit in large independent outcome trials, is mature and confirmed over decades. The chair's first question is the one that matters. I would have the citation reward the discovery of how GLP-1 works as a hormone and the identity of its active form, with the therapeutic arc as the evidence that the field changed. That reading fits a prize for a specific discovery rather than for a product. Holst (human physiology), Drucker (proglucagon-derived peptide and receptor biology in vivo) and Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active peptide) are three distinct steps in the discovery and remain my preferred names.
statement.case_against: The weakness is attribution, and I have not resolved it. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36/37) peptide relative to Habener and others is contested, and I have not checked it against primary documents, as none of us has. The three-person cap also leaves out Knudsen, whose analogue design made the peptide a drug, so a discovery-only trio can be read as honouring the biology and omitting the therapy. If the priority record cannot be defended in committee, my configuration would be weaker than the Drucker, Holst, Knudsen alternative, and I would accept that alternative. There is also a risk that the prize follows the most visible clinical story, and clean two-person attributions such as B016 are fairer on credit alone.

responses.point: Svenningsson and Sandberg keep Knudsen as the third name, arguing that without half-life extension the physiology would not have become a medicine, and that a citation naming both discovery and development is more faithful to what changed medicine.
responses.response: That argument has force and I have moved toward it. I still do not think half-life engineering is the discovery this prize should centre on, because the recognised step is understanding what GLP-1 is and does, and the analogue work is a team effort with a large proprietary component. Naming Knudsen would also make this an award for development, and I think the committee should say so openly instead of reaching it by default. My position is a decision rule. I keep Mojsov if the record shows she can be defended for the active peptide, and I switch to Knudsen if it does not. I would not block your configuration if that is where the majority settles, since all of us agree on Drucker and Holst.

responses.point: Sandberg says a Drucker, Holst, Mojsov trio is defensible and would not block it, but worries that choosing Mojsov entangles the committee in a priority dispute the record does not settle, while Knudsen is the pharmacological translator.
responses.response: I agree that the dispute is real and that the committee should not take Mojsov on trust. My answer is that an unsettled priority question does not by itself remove her. The citation can be written around what was established, the physiology and the active form of the peptide, and a citation drawn that way does not depend on settling every priority claim against Habener. If it cannot be drawn that way, then your Knudsen configuration is the safer one and I would support it. I would also say that choosing Knudsen only because the record is messy would be a choice by default, and I would want it argued as a decision about what the prize is for.

responses.point: El-Manira keeps the discovery-only trio but says the Drucker, Holst, Knudsen configuration is the safer choice if the priority record is unclear, and notes that B016 or B019 would be cleaner on attribution if the GLP-1 credit split proves unresolvable.
responses.response: I agree with your fallback ordering, and your point that the fallback should be the Knudsen trio and not a different achievement is right. If the GLP-1 credit split were truly unresolvable, I would not abandon B006, because the science is the most robust on the list and the issue is only the third name. Moving to B016 or B019 only because the attribution is easier would reward clean credit over the size of the change in the field. I would keep both as alternatives. B016 is a fundamental mechanism with clean credit, but the disease link is largely correlative. B019 has a larger attribution problem than B006, since Eshhar and others are outside the credited names.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius moved B006 ahead of B001 after her opening ranking, but notes that a GLP-1 prize would leave the equally mature TNF blockade (B001) unrecognised, with a cleaner two-person attribution, and asks whether a two-part prize is possible.
responses.response: I take the point that B001 is mature and has a cleaner credit line. I still question what the credited step is, the demonstration that TNF drives synovial inflammation or the later antibody engineering and development, and I do not think the committee has settled that. A B006 plus B001 prize is arithmetically possible only by cutting GLP-1 to one name and B001 to two, which would break the Drucker and Holst anchors that everyone shares. I therefore keep a single prize part this year and hold B001 as a serious candidate for a later year, when the TNF credit question has been examined more closely.

uncertainties: Whether the documentary record lets the committee defend Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36/37) peptide relative to Habener and others. I cannot verify this from the material supplied, and it decides whether I stay with Mojsov or move to Knudsen.

Whether the committee explicitly wants a discovery-only citation or one that also rewards drug development, and whether crediting an industry scientist is a matter of principle or only follows from who made the decisive contribution.
Whether a two-part prize is worth it if it forces Drucker and Holst to share a part with a third GLP-1 name unrepresented, given the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific conflict. My documented work (nuclear receptors, Nurr1, dopamine neurons) does not overlap with GLP-1. I co-authored nuclear-receptor work with Ronald Evans and collaborated with Johan Ericson, and neither is credited on any shortlisted ballot. I also share about twenty co-authored works with the chair, Per Svenningsson, and one with El-Manira (2009), none concerning a shortlisted candidate or credited name. This does not change my disclosure from round 1 beyond stating these links explicitly.
